Russia’s ruling pro-Putin party on track to win wartime election after drones strike Moscow

Reuters

21 September, 2026 01:30 am IST

Facebook

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

By Andrew Osborn and Vladimir Soldatkin MOSCOW, Sept 20 (Reuters) – Russia’s ruling United Russia party was on track to easily win a parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in Ukraine, partial official results showed on Sunday, after Ukraine launched a massive drone attack on the Russian capital.

In a tightly controlled political system which critics say does not tolerate genuine dissent, initial results showed United Russia comfortably ahead with 57.5% of the vote. Other parties like the Communists, the ultra-nationalist LDPR, the New People party and the Just Russia party  – who all vote the same way as United Russia on major issues – trailed by a huge margin but were on course to win seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament.

Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council and a former president, was quick to declare that United Russia had performed with dignity, a result he said showed that Russians had entrusted it to govern further.

Show Full Article

Russian government officials accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt the State Duma vote – the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 – after Kyiv launched hundreds of drones at Moscow and other regions in what the TASS state news agency said was the biggest attack of its kind since the war began.

The drone strikes killed three people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine’s Kherson region, including an election official, according to the region’s governor and the election commission.

A facility at Moscow’s oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged. As voting got underway in the capital, flames and huge columns of smoke rose from the site on its outskirts.

“The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled,” Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed.”

Russia’s Defence Ministry said Ukraine had also fired Flamingo cruise missiles and said it had downed nearly 2,000 Ukrainian drones targeting various regions and 8 cruise missiles in the last 24 hours. It said it would intensify its own strikes on Ukrainian military targets in response.

VOTING SYSTEMS HIT BY CYBER ATTACKS, SAY OFFICIALS

Voting systems also faced waves of cyber attacks, according to election authorities, who said that the electoral process had nonetheless been mostly smooth.

Russia’s opposition in exile had called on those who opposed the authorities to stand in line at voting stations at noon to express their dissent, a call which saw long lines form in some locations. It was unclear, however, what impact that had on the overall outcome.

The Kremlin is likely to present the results as evidence of public backing for Putin’s policies and for the war, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.

Central Election Commission Chairwoman (CEC) Ella Pamfilova said the latest attacks had not deterred voters. “The more pressure they put on us, the more we are seeing an unprecedented level of what I would call public unity,” RIA news agency quoted her as saying.

Turnout had reached nearly 57% as of early evening Moscow time, CEC data showed.

Most anti-war candidates have been barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict.

Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences.

In a small act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace”.

The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine. It casts the conflict – Europe’s deadliest since World War Two – as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West. Moscow says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.

PERMITTED OPPOSITION PARTIES COULD BENEFIT

Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election”.

Despite what experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated “a foreign agent”, said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.

It said the Communist party and the New People party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia.

“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot,” it said in a note.

(Reporting by ReutersWriting by Andrew Osborn and Alessandra Prentice Editing by Kirsten Donovan, Ros Russell, Toby Chopra)

South African journalist missing in Djibouti, family says

Reuters

21 September, 2026 12:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

JOHANNESBURG, Sept 20 (Reuters) – South African investigative journalist Micah Reddy has gone missing in Djibouti while on a reporting trip, his family said on Sunday, adding that they have received no information from authorities about his whereabouts since he was last heard from on Saturday.

Reddy, the Africa editor for the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), arrived in the Horn of Africa nation on Thursday and had been in regular contact with family and colleagues before communication abruptly ceased, his brother Niall Reddy told Reuters on Sunday.

“We don’t have any clear updates on his status,” Niall said.

Show Full Article

The Committee to Protect Journalists watchdog said in a post on X that it was “increasingly alarmed” that over 24 hours had elapsed since anyone had been able to reach Reddy or his fixer, Kooki Mahmoud.

“CPJ understands their reporting was not focused on Djibouti and urges Djiboutian authorities to establish their whereabouts, credibly confirm their safety, and promptly release them if detained,” Angela Quintal, CPJ Africa Director, said in a statement posted on X.

Niall said Micah’s last contact with him was around 11 a.m. on Saturday, while his last known communication with colleagues was at about 1 p.m. the same day. Several hours later, messages sent to him via Signal and WhatsApp were no longer being delivered, prompting concern among relatives and colleagues.

Micah was staying at the Escale International hotel in Djibouti’s capital and was last known to have met Mahmoud in the hotel lobby, according to his family. Relatives said the hotel had provided little information about his movements after he was last seen.

Niall said his brother had not reported any threats before the trip and was not investigating the Djiboutian government during his visit.

He added that South African and British officials had sought information from Djibouti’s government following the journalist’s disappearance, but the family had so far received no clarity on his whereabouts and no official comment from authorities.

A senior official in the Djibouti presidency, Naguib Ali Taher, said that Micah had not registered for media accreditation in Djibouti.

“We need to check the tourist visa records to see if he came to Djibouti,” he said.

A spokesperson for the South African government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

(Reporting by Nqobile Dludla, Aaron Ross and Ammu Kannampilly; Editing by Nick Zieminski)

Harry and Meghan need protection to avoid Diana’s ordeal, her brother Spencer says

Reuters

21 September, 2026 12:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Kate Holton LONDON, Sept 20 (Reuters) – The brother of Princess Diana said her son, Prince Harry, and his American wife Meghan should be given official security as they are now treated by the media much in the same way as his late sister was in the years leading up to her death.

Diana died aged 36 in a 1997 Paris car crash as photographers pursued her on motorbikes, sparking an outpouring of grief and a reckoning over whether the media bore some responsibility after it splashed details of her life across front pages for years.

Charles Spencer was speaking as he prepared to publish his book about Diana, which has been highly critical of her former husband, the now-King Charles, and after Harry and Meghan returned to live in Britain six years after they quit royal duties and moved to the US.

Show Full Article

“From a security aspect, as an uncle who’s seen his sister die in very, very preventable circumstances, I would veer towards protection,” Charles Spencer told the BBC, citing Harry’s position as fifth-in-line to the British throne and as a former soldier.

He said the tabloid treatment of both Diana, and Harry and Meghan, could be “really, really unpleasant”, that it was “beholden on people” to learn from that experience.

SPENCER’S BOOK MAKES HEADLINES AROUND THE WORLD

Spencer’s book: “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister”, has made headlines around the world after it accused the now-King Charles of making incendiary comments in the days after the death.

In the book Spencer accused Diana’s former husband, the then-prince of Wales, of sounding “giddily elated” in the hours after her death and said an angry Charles had told Spencer that the world would forget Diana soon enough.

In a rare move, the palace hit back by saying the king was “mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”.

Asked by the BBC how he could prove the conversations had taken place, Spencer said he had included a specific line in his much-lauded eulogy at Diana’s funeral to counter the comments, ending it by saying she would “never be extinguished from our minds”.

Spencer said he had written the book, ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death, to celebrate her life. He said their childhood had never had a dull moment: “We both have ADHD. She was never diagnosed, but clearly we did”.

The publication of the book and the surprise return of Harry and Meghan to Britain after they spent six years living in the US pose a challenge for the king, who is still undergoing treatment for cancer.

Diana’s family accused the royals of showing a lack of support or care towards the late princess before her death, a charge that was repeated by Harry and Meghan before they quit royal duties in 2020 to move abroad.

Harry has criticised the government’s decision to strip him and his family of automatic police protection afforded to other senior royals, after he quit royal duties. Following a long-running legal battle, that is now under review.

Spencer, who recently hosted the couple, has serialised his book through the Daily Mail, just months after Harry lost an expensive privacy lawsuit against the tabloid.

Spencer said his revelations about Charles would not come as a surprise to Harry or his older brother, the heir-to-the-throne Prince William, and said while he knew many more details about the king he had chosen not to include them.

(Reporting by Kate Holton; Editing by Helen Popper, Toby Chopra)

Trump’s Greenland deal changes little. His bullying can change US-Denmark ties

As Donald Trump ended his confrontation over Greenland, European leaders were remembering the enormous risks taken as the Cold War began to descend on their borders.

Praveen Swami

20 September, 2026 05:05 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of US President Donald Trump | Daniel Heuer | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

E ight metres below the endless darkness of the Arctic winter, there were hot showers, flush toilets and a cafeteria serving double portions of steak and ice cream. The 21 tunnels cut into the ice sheet of northern Greenland in 1959 were to have grown into a 1,25,000 square-kilometre secret city , housing hundreds of nuclear missiles aimed at the Soviet Union. Even as winds exceeding 200 kilometres per hour lashed the surface and temperatures fell below minus 50°C, the portable PM2A nuclear reactor powering the ice city ensured it was always summer inside.

“Life inside the mile-thick glacier is not too different from that in many small US, Canadian or British towns,” a visitor recorded : Even if those towns were annihilated in a nuclear war, civilisation would live on under the ice.

However, t here was one small catch: The Social Democratic coalition that had won Denmark’s 1957 election had vowed, in writing, not to allow nuclear weapons to be stationed on its soil. The decision followed a threat made by Soviet Prime Minister Nikolai Bulganin earlier that year: “For countries the size of Denmark, the granting to foreign powers of the possibility of establishing bases would, in the event of the outbreak of an atomic war, be synonymous with suicide.”

Show Full Article

Last week, as US President Donald Trump ended his months-long confrontation over Greenland by gloating over what he claims to be a historic new agreement, European leaders were remembering the enormous risks taken as the Cold War began to descend on their borders.

Fearing that its North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) allies might break ranks over the deployment of nuclear weapons in Europe, the State Department ordered its ambassador to Denmark to meet Prime Minister Hans Christian Hansen.

Even though he’d heard about “the possible storing of supplies of munition of a special kind in the defence areas in Greenland,” Hansen responded, the Denmark government had not been presented with concrete plans or asked about its attitudes. The equipment the United States chose to store on its bases was, in any case, “permitted entry into Greenland free of inspection.”

As long as he was told nothing, Hansen was saying, he was willing to allow nuclear missiles to be stationed at American bases in Greenland, and risk Soviet wrath.

New words, old wars The text of the new Greenland agreement hasn’t been released, but officials have said it gives America “permanent access, basing and overflights rights,” as well as the “unilateral power to build additional military structures.” The agreement is also thought to contain provisions barring adversaries of the US —like China or Russia—from deploying troops in Greenland, or making investments in strategic sectors. Trump claimed the agreement allowed the US to address its security concerns at “no cost to the United States.”

All of this would be a significant victory—if it hadn’t already been won in 1951. For little more than a few moments of social media bragging, Trump has taken a hammer to the trust built over generations.

The Defence of Greenland Treaty of 1951 gave the US the right to control airspace and anchorage over designated defence areas. The kingdom also ceded its right to enforce its laws against, and to collect taxes from, American military personnel. The Treaty was to stay in effect as long as the North Atlantic Treaty, which had no date of expiry. Laws subjecting foreign investments in Denmark to security screening were put in place in 2021. Greenland began working on a similar legal framework three years later .

From as early as November 1945—eight weeks after the end of the Second World War—American war planners began preparing the first drafts of their nuclear war doctrine , as part of a thoroughgoing study of Soviet military capabilities. These early efforts had crystallised by 1946, when a plan drawn up for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, recommending expansion of America’s nuclear arsenal, concluded that nuclear weapons could “nullify any nation’s military effort and demolish its social and economic structures.”

America’s nuclear arsenal was small—growing from nine warheads in 1945 to 56 in 1948—but the country’s leadership believed it offered a means to offset Western deficits in numbers. Greenland and Iceland were critical elements of nuclear deterrence. Few aircraft could fly transatlantic, and refuelling bases were needed along polar routes. Those routes also enabled surveillance of the Soviet submarine fleet.

The February 1948 coup in Czechoslovakia, followed by the blockade of West Berlin, persuaded former US President Harry Truman that the Soviets had to be confronted . That summer, he d i spatched B-29 bombers to Europe—a declaration of willingness to use nuclear weapons to defend America’s allies.

Europeans were not universally persuaded of the wisdom of the emerging doctrine of nuclear deterrence. The US believed that stationing nuclear weapons on the territory of NATO partners would strengthen deterrence. To both Denmark and Norway, though, there seemed a real risk that nuclear weapons stationed on their soil might invite attack. A complex series of negotiations followed, carving out an exception in Greenland: The language of Danish sovereignty would not apply to American defence zones on the island.

Also read: Trump threatened to redraw the map. Greenland deal shows the limits of his disruption

The Wholesale e mpire The Arctic Eden had, in fact, been bid for long before the Cold War: the sea, a determined buyer’s brochure recorded , was awash with “whale, walrus, seal, and shark, cod, ivory-cod, salmon, salmon-trout, and herring; foxes, wolf, reindeer, bear, hare, myriads of birds, including the king duck, eider duck, dorskin, petrel, gull, brent, burgo-master, goose, killiwoke, lolard, and sea swallow.”

Like most marketing material, the text had raced just a little ahead of reality: “Killiwoke,” likely a misspelling of kiviak, was a dish made of fermented seabirds, not a kind of wildlife. There was, it was true, enough coal to power a merchant fleet and summer routes across the Bering Strait from Europe to East Asia.

Long before Trump and rare-earth metals lobbyists began pushing the idea, US Secretary of State William Seward—the force behind the purchase of Alaska for $7.2 million—decided Iceland and Greenland should be added to the American empire.

To Seward and other American imperialists, their case was unassailable —and not because of the wildlife. American naval power would be able to flank what an 1868 g overnment publication called British America—the territory that had become Canada the previous year. Like Trump, Seward believed that control of the territory off Canada’s eastern coast would “greatly increase her inducements, peacefully and cheerfully, to become a part of the American Union.”

Few in America, though, were keen to buy. The problem was that Americans didn’t want their taxes spent buying what the newspapers were starting to call a Polar Bear Garden, an Ice-Box, or, even more unkindly, Seward’s Folly. The discovery of gold and oil in Alaska was still decades away.

The idea didn’t disappear. In 1910, America’s ambassador to Denmark, Maurice Egan, proposed a territorial swap , which would have restored the European principality of Schleswig-Holstein to Denmark, in return for a cluster of Philippine islands America would have given to Germany. Then, in 1940, Germany invaded Denmark. The US responded by occupying Greenland, and asserting that the island was covered by the Monroe Doctrine—the American declaration prohibiting any foreign strategic presence in the Western Hemisphere.

Enemies had changed, more than once, through the 20th century—but geography hadn’t. The question was how leaders of the transatlantic alliance could reconcile conflicting aims and values to protect their shared interests.

Also read: The 2026 midterms will test the political foundations of American power abroad

Friends and lovers Geography is changing, though—and that change underpins the growing strategic significance of Greenland. The Arctic sea routes will be ice-free throughout the year before the middle of this century, opening up fast routes between ports in China, Russia and America’s western seaboard. The ice-city built in 1959 had to be abandoned within two decades because the enormous pressure exerted by the shifting ice sheet crushed the tunnels.

The melting of the ice sheets over Greenland, though, will make mining for rare-earth metals and hydrocarbons commercially viable. The question is: Was it really necessary for the US to assert sovereignty over Greenland to secure its interests and regulate the new regional order?

The story of the transatlantic relationship offers us a simple answer. Throughout the Cold War, the Danish leadership went to extraordinary lengths to protect and nurture their relationship with NATO and the US.

Following the crash of a B-52 bomber off Thule in 1968—which led to a cloud of radioactive material from its four nuclear bombs being spewed over the ice-bound port—the US agreed to demands for Greenland to become a nuclear-free zone. This was, in part, because nuclear submarines and ballistic missiles had made conventional bombers irrelevant. For their part, Danish authorities agreed to language that would allow nuclear weapons back on Greenland in some circumstances.

Leaders in both Washington and Copenhagen understood that their alliance was anchored in one core interest: the need to defend themselves against the Soviet Union. To do so, however, they had to make complex compromises, sometimes even resorting to lies and deceit. The solutions, though, emerged from hard-won trust, not braggadocio or bullying.

Praveen Swami is a Contributing Editor at ThePrint. His X handle is @praveenswami. Views are personal.

(Edited by Saptak Datta)
